title: The Genealogy and Birth of Jesus the Messiah
summary: Matthew opens with the family line of Jesus, traced from Abraham through King David and the exile to Joseph, arranged in three sets of fourteen generations and including four women from Israel's past. Then he tells how Mary, engaged to Joseph, was found to be pregnant through the Holy Spirit. An angel tells Joseph in a dream to take Mary as his wife and to name the child Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins, fulfilling Isaiah's promise of Immanuel, God with us.
story:
The Old Testament closed with Israel home from exile but still waiting: no king on David's throne, foreign empires in charge, and Malachi's promise of a coming messenger unanswered. Matthew's first line picks up the whole story at once. By calling Jesus the son of David and the son of Abraham, he ties him to the two great promises of the Old Testament, the covenant with Abraham that all nations would be blessed through his offspring (Genesis 12:3; 22:18) and the covenant with David that his throne would last forever (2 Samuel 7:12-16).

The genealogy then retells Israel's history in names. It rises from Abraham to David the king, falls through the long line of kings into the disaster of the exile to Babylon, and waits through a list of names otherwise unknown to Scripture until the Messiah arrives. A reader who knew the Scriptures would hear the whole story of the Old Testament compressed into seventeen verses, with its heroes and its failures left in. The birth account that follows shows that this son of David enters the royal line in an unexpected way: by legal adoption through Joseph, a descendant of David, and by the power of the Holy Spirit, without a human father. The chapter answers the question of who Jesus is; chapter 2 will answer where he comes from and how the world receives him.
historical:
The events are set in the last years of Herod the Great, whom Rome made king of Judea and who died, on the usual reckoning from Josephus, in 4 BC; a minority of scholars, following W. E. Filmer (Journal of Theological Studies, 1966) and Andrew Steinmann (Novum Testamentum, 2009), argue for 1 BC. Jesus was therefore born a few years before the year numbered AD 1. The system of counting years from his birth was worked out by the monk Dionysius Exiguus in Rome around 525 for his Easter tables, and his calculation missed by several years. Luke places Joseph and Mary in Nazareth before the birth; Matthew first mentions Nazareth when the family settles there after returning from Egypt (2:23).

Genealogies mattered in Second Temple Judaism. Priests had to prove their descent to serve (Ezra 2:61-63), and the historian Josephus opens his Life (1-6) by setting out his own priestly pedigree as he found it in the public registers. Descent from David was remembered too. Julius Africanus, writing in the early third century and quoted by Eusebius (Church History 1.7.11-14), reports that relatives of Jesus in Galilee kept private family records after Herod had destroyed the public ones, and Hegesippus (in Eusebius, Church History 3.19-20) tells of grandsons of Jesus' brother Jude brought before the emperor Domitian as descendants of David. A royal pedigree could be dangerous as well as honorable.

The genealogy's turning point is the exile. In 597 BC Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon took King Jeconiah (also called Jehoiachin or Coniah) captive with the leading families of Jerusalem (2 Kings 24:8-17); in 587 or 586 BC the city and temple were destroyed. Clay ration lists from Nebuchadnezzar's palace, published by Ernst Weidner in 1939, record oil issued to Ya'ukinu, king of Judah, and his sons in Babylon, and 2 Kings 25:27-30 tells of his release from prison by Evil-merodach around 561 BC. His son Shealtiel (1 Chronicles 3:17) and grandson Zerubbabel, governor of Judah when the second temple was rebuilt around 520 to 515 BC (Haggai 1:1; Ezra 3:8), are the last names in Matthew's list that appear in the Old Testament; 1 Chronicles 3:19 calls Zerubbabel a son of Pedaiah, Shealtiel's brother, perhaps through a levirate marriage. The nine names from Abiud to Jacob (verses 13 to 15) are otherwise unknown, and the six centuries between Zerubbabel and Jesus are covered in only a few generations.

Luke's genealogy (Luke 3:23-38) runs backward from Jesus to Adam and follows David's son Nathan rather than Solomon; between David and Joseph it shares only Shealtiel and Zerubbabel with Matthew, and it names Joseph's father Heli rather than Jacob. Julius Africanus, in his Letter to Aristides (Eusebius, Church History 1.7), explained the difference by a levirate marriage (a man marrying his dead brother's widow to raise children in the brother's name, Deuteronomy 25:5-6), so that Joseph had a natural and a legal father. Others hold that Luke gives Mary's line and Matthew Joseph's, or that Matthew traces the royal succession and Luke the natural descent. Many critical scholars, Raymond Brown among them, doubt that the lists can be harmonized and think each evangelist drew on a different tradition for his own purpose.
cultural:
A Jewish marriage came in two stages. First came betrothal (erusin or kiddushin), a binding agreement made before witnesses, often with a payment or a written deed; the Mishnah (Kiddushin 1:1) lists money, a document, or intercourse as the ways a wife was acquired. From betrothal the couple were legally husband and wife (Matthew calls Joseph her husband in verse 19 and Mary his wife in verse 20), and only a divorce could end the bond, though they did not yet live together. About a year later (the Mishnah, Ketubbot 5:2, allows a betrothed virgin twelve months to prepare) came the wedding, when the husband took the bride into his home. Mary was found pregnant between the two stages. Under the law of Moses a betrothed woman who lay with another man could be put to death (Deuteronomy 22:23-24), and a husband who suspected his wife could bring her to the priest for the ordeal of the bitter water (Numbers 5:11-31); the Mishnah (Sotah 9:9) says Yohanan ben Zakkai ended that rite after AD 70. In Roman Judea the death penalty was probably not carried out for this, and the usual outcome was divorce and public disgrace. Joseph chooses a quiet divorce, before the minimum of witnesses, rather than a public accusation.

Naming mattered. When Joseph gives the child his name (verses 21 and 25), he acknowledges him as his son, and the child enters Joseph's line, the line of David, with full legal standing. The name itself was common: Yeshua, a later form of Joshua, meaning the LORD saves, and Josephus names a number of men called Jesus. Dreams were an accepted channel of divine guidance, and Matthew's Joseph is a dreamer whose father is named Jacob and who will take his family down to Egypt, like the patriarch Joseph son of Jacob in Genesis 37 to 50.

Genealogies in the ancient world were not neutral records. They claimed status, inheritance, and identity, and they often skipped generations. Women were rarely named, which makes Matthew's four striking. Tamar, whose people Genesis does not give (the book of Jubilees 41:1 makes her an Aramean), bore twins to her father-in-law Judah after he refused her his son, and Judah confessed that she was more righteous than he (Genesis 38:26). Rahab was a Canaanite of Jericho who sheltered Israel's spies (Joshua 2 and 6); no Old Testament text makes her the mother of Boaz, and a rabbinic tradition (Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 14b) married her instead to Joshua. Ruth was a Moabite, from a people barred from the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:3), who became the great-grandmother of David (Ruth 4:17). Bathsheba is not named at all but called “Uriah’s wife” (verse 6), keeping in view Uriah the Hittite, whom David had killed after taking her (2 Samuel 11 and 12). Each woman was an outsider or joined to one, and each union was irregular in a way that the people of God later honored.
literary:
The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 17 are a genealogy; verses 18 to 25 are the story of the birth, told from Joseph's side. The heading, “the record of the genealogy” (biblos geneseōs, literally the book of the genesis), echoes the Greek of Genesis 2:4 and 5:1, and the word genesis returns in verse 18 (“This is how the birth of Jesus Christ came about”), binding the two parts together. Scholars debate whether the heading introduces the genealogy, the infancy narrative, or the whole book; the echo of Genesis suggests a new beginning in any case.

The list is built in three sections of fourteen generations, as verse 17 says: from Abraham to David, from David to the exile, and from the exile to the Christ. The pattern, A was the father of B, repeats about forty times with the verb egennēsen. The arrangement is deliberate. Matthew leaves out Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah between Joram and Uzziah (compare 1 Chronicles 3:11-12) and Jehoiakim between Josiah and Jeconiah, who was Josiah's grandson. Many interpreters think fourteen was chosen because the Hebrew consonants of David's name (D-W-D) have the numerical values 4, 6, and 4, which add up to fourteen; David is the fourteenth name, and the only one given a title, “David the king” (verse 6). The count of the third section is a puzzle, since it has only thirteen generations unless Jeconiah is counted in both the second and third groups, or Jesus and the Christ are counted separately; no solution has won general agreement. Some also note that three fourteens make six sevens, placing Jesus at the start of the seventh seven, though Matthew does not say so.

Two things break the pattern. The four women interrupt the chain of fathers, and at verse 16 the formula changes: Jacob was the father of Joseph, “the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus”. The Greek relative pronoun (ex hēs) is feminine, and the verb shifts to the passive (egennēthē, was born), so that Joseph is not said to have fathered Jesus. The genealogy ends on a question that verses 18 to 25 answer. That narrative moves in three steps: the problem (verses 18 and 19), the angel's message in a dream (verses 20 to 23), and Joseph's obedience (verses 24 and 25). It contains the first of Matthew's fulfillment formulas, “All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet” (verse 22), which recurs about ten times in the Gospel, and it is framed by the child's two names: Jesus, given by Joseph (verses 21 and 25), and Immanuel, spoken by the prophet (verse 23).

outline.t: Title: Jesus the Messiah, son of David, son of Abraham
From the exile to the Messiah
Mary is found with child; Joseph's decision
The angel's message and the Immanuel prophecy
Joseph obeys and names the child Jesus

doctrines.note: Jesus is named the Christ, the anointed king, in the first verse and presented as the heir of the promises to Abraham and David. Through Joseph's acknowledgment he is legally the son of David, and the genealogy shows Israel's history moving toward him, through its glory and its collapse.

The child is conceived “through the Holy Spirit” (verse 18) without a human father and named Immanuel, God with us (verse 23). The church's creeds confess from this chapter and Luke 1 that the Son was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, one person truly God and truly human, and that he entered a real family history with its failures.

The first fulfillment formula (verse 22) sets the pattern of the Gospel: the events of Jesus' life complete what God said through the prophets. Here Isaiah 7:14, a sign given to King Ahaz, is read as reaching its fullness in Jesus; how the original sign relates to its fulfillment is discussed under the hard questions.

The angel explains the name Jesus, the LORD saves: “He will save His people from their sins” (verse 21). Matthew defines the Messiah's rescue first as rescue from sin, not only from Rome, and the Gospel will show it accomplished in the blood of the covenant poured out for the forgiveness of sins (26:28).

The Holy Spirit is named twice as the source of the conception (verses 18 and 20), recalling the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2). The same Spirit will descend on Jesus at his baptism (3:16), and the Gospel ends with the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (28:19).

words.note: Genesis, origin, beginning, birth, lineage. It occurs only five times in the New Testament, twice in this chapter (verses 1 and 18) and twice in James (1:23, 3:6). The phrase biblos geneseōs appears in the Greek Old Testament at Genesis 2:4 and 5:1, and Matthew's use invites the reader to hear a new beginning, a new genesis, in the coming of Jesus. In verse 18 later manuscripts read the more ordinary gennēsis, birth.

Gennaō, to beget, father, bear, or in the passive to be born. It occurs about 97 times in the New Testament, and 45 of them are in Matthew, nearly forty in this genealogy. In verse 16 the active form, used of every father in the list, gives way to the passive, was born, and in verse 20 the passive participle (to gennēthen, what has been conceived) describes the child conceived from the Holy Spirit. The grammar carries the point: Joseph did not beget Jesus.

Metoikesia, deportation, removal to another home. It appears only four times in the New Testament, all in verses 11, 12, and 17 of this chapter. By making the exile one of the three turning points of the genealogy, Matthew implies that Israel's story still waited for the end of exile, which the Messiah would bring.

Dikaios, righteous, just. It occurs about 79 times in the New Testament and 17 times in Matthew, more than in any other book. BDAG describes it as conforming to the standard of what God requires. Joseph is called righteous (verse 19), and interpreters debate whether his righteousness is shown by his intention to divorce (keeping the law) or by his choice to do it quietly (mercy); many hold that Matthew means both, a righteousness that keeps the law without cruelty, which the Gospel later calls justice, mercy, and faithfulness (23:23).

Parthenos, virgin, a young woman who has not had sexual relations. It occurs fifteen times in the New Testament. Isaiah 7:14 in Hebrew uses almah, a young woman of marriageable age, but the Greek translation of Isaiah, made by Jews before the Christian era, used parthenos, and Matthew quotes that translation. Parthenos usually implies virginity, though the Greek of Genesis 34:3 uses it of Dinah after she had been violated. Matthew's own narrative makes his meaning plain in verses 18, 20, and 25.

Sōzō, to save, rescue, keep safe, heal. It occurs about 107 times in the New Testament and 16 times in Matthew, where it covers rescue from drowning (8:25, 14:30), healing (9:21-22), and final salvation (10:22, 24:13). The angel ties it to the name Jesus (Iēsous, from the Hebrew Yeshua or Joshua, the LORD saves) and defines its object: his people's sins. On the cross the mockers will use the same verb, “He saved others, but He cannot save Himself” (27:42), without knowing why it was true.

Emmanouēl, Immanuel, the Greek form of the Hebrew immanu el, God with us, as Matthew translates. It occurs only here in the New Testament. In Isaiah the name appears in 7:14 and 8:8, and the phrase God is with us closes 8:10. Matthew frames his whole Gospel with the idea: the child is God with us here, and the risen Jesus promises “I am with you always” in the last verse (28:20). The name is a title of what he is, not what he was called in daily life, where he was Jesus.

christ:
Matthew's first chapter answers the question of who Jesus is with three claims. He is the son of David, the rightful king of Israel, heir to the promise that David's throne would stand forever (2 Samuel 7:13) and to the prophets' hope for a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1). He is the son of Abraham, the one through whom “all the families of the earth will be blessed” (Genesis 12:3), which is why a Gospel that begins with Abraham ends with a command to make disciples of all nations. And he is Immanuel, God with us, conceived by the Holy Spirit.

The fulfillment formula of verse 22 introduces Isaiah 7:14: “Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”). In Isaiah the sign was given to the house of David when King Ahaz refused to trust God, and the child's name promised that God would be with his people through the Assyrian storm (Isaiah 8:8-10). The prophecy continues into the promise of a child who will reign on the throne of David, called “Mighty God” (Isaiah 9:6-7). Matthew reads the whole passage as reaching its goal in Jesus: the sign to David's house is fulfilled in David's true son, and God with us is no longer only a promise of help but a person.

The two names in the chapter belong together. Jesus names what he will do, save his people from their sins; Immanuel names who he is, God present with his people. The church has confessed from its earliest creeds that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, and has seen in this the mystery of one person truly God and truly human. The genealogy shows the kind of Savior he is. Its names include liars and adulterers, idolaters like Manasseh, a Moabite widow and a Canaanite harlot, a king carried off in chains, and nine men no one remembers. Jesus does not enter humanity above its history but through it, taking a family line with its sins so that he might save his people from them.
interpretation:
The genealogy and the virgin conception have been read and contested from the second century. Justin Martyr's Dialogue with Trypho (around 160) shows the Jewish objection already fully formed: Trypho says the Hebrew of Isaiah 7:14 means a young woman, that the child was Hezekiah, and that the Christian story resembles the Greek myth of Danaë (Dialogue 43, 67, 71). Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.21.1) complains that Theodotion and Aquila, Jewish translators of the second century, rendered the word ‘young woman’; Symmachus's translation did the same. The pagan critic Celsus, quoted by Origen (Against Celsus 1.28, 1.32), repeated a Jewish story that Mary was put out by her husband for adultery with a soldier named Panthera, and the name ben Pantera appears in the Tosefta (Hullin 2:22-24). Origen answered him, and Ignatius of Antioch (To the Ephesians 19) already counted Mary's virginity among the mysteries hidden from the ruler of this age. The Old Roman Creed and the Apostles' Creed confess that Jesus was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

Verse 25 became the text of a later debate. The Protevangelium of James (mid-second century) presented Mary as ever-virgin and Jesus' brothers as Joseph's sons by an earlier marriage, a view Epiphanius defended. Helvidius in Rome argued from verse 25 and 13:55 that Mary later bore other children, and Jerome answered him (Against Helvidius, around 383) that the brothers were cousins. Most Protestants in modern times have taken Helvidius's view, though Luther held Mary's perpetual virginity and Calvin declined to press the question; Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold Mary's perpetual virginity.

On the four women, Jerome's Commentary on Matthew (398) called them sinners, placed there to show that Christ came to save sinners; Luther saw them as foreigners, a sign that Christ belongs to the Gentiles too. Raymond Brown (The Birth of the Messiah, 1977) combined the readings: each union was irregular yet part of God's plan, preparing for Mary. Jane Schaberg (The Illegitimacy of Jesus, 1987) argued that Matthew was answering a tradition of illegitimate birth. Jewish readers of the Hebrew Bible kept their own readings of Isaiah 7:14: Rashi and David Kimhi (Radak) identified the young woman as the wife of the prophet or of the king.

In art the genealogy became the Tree of Jesse, drawn from Isaiah 11:1: a vine rising from the sleeping Jesse through the kings to Mary and Christ, as in the twelfth-century window of the west front of Chartres Cathedral, and Michelangelo painted Matthew's ancestors of Christ in the lunettes of the Sistine Chapel (1508 to 1512). In the Roman lectionary the genealogy is read on 17 December, when the final days of Advent begin, and the whole chapter at the Vigil Mass of Christmas; the Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 18 to 25 on the Fourth Sunday of Advent in Year A. Krister Stendahl's essay Quis et Unde (1960) gave modern study its formula for chapters 1 and 2: chapter 1 answers who Jesus is, chapter 2 where he comes from.
text:
The chapter is attested early: P1 (P.Oxy. 2, early third century, in the University of Pennsylvania Museum) preserves much of verses 1 to 20 in a text close to Codex Vaticanus.

In verses 7 and 8 the earliest manuscripts (P1, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and others) spell the king's name Asaph, the name of the psalmist, where later manuscripts read Asa, the king of 1 Kings 15. In verse 10 many of the same witnesses read Amos, the name of the prophet, for King Amon. Critical editions print Asaph and Amos; most English Bibles, including the BSB, translate Asa and Amon, sometimes with a note. Some scholars think the spellings are early copying errors; others think Matthew or his source followed a form of the Greek Old Testament with these spellings, and a few suggest he deliberately included a psalmist and a prophet in the line of Christ.

Verse 16 has the most discussed variant. Nearly all manuscripts read as the BSB does. A small group (Codex Koridethi, family 13, and some Old Latin) reads ‘Joseph, to whom the virgin Mary, being betrothed, bore Jesus’, and the Sinaitic Syriac reads ‘Joseph, to whom was betrothed Mary the virgin, fathered Jesus’. The Syriac still calls Mary a virgin and keeps verses 18 to 25; most scholars think it uses the genealogy's legal language rather than denying the virgin conception, and no modern edition adopts it. In verse 18 later manuscripts read gennēsis (birth) for genesis (origin), and some read ‘Christ Jesus’ or ‘Christ’. In verse 25 the King James Version reads ‘her firstborn son’, from later manuscripts that borrowed the phrase from Luke 2:7; Sinaiticus and Vaticanus read ‘a son’.

teach.big: Jesus is the son of David and son of Abraham to whom Israel's whole history leads, and he comes into that history as God with us, conceived by the Holy Spirit, to save his people from their sins.

outline.t: Matthew opens with a title that names Jesus as Christ, son of David, and son of Abraham, the heir of both great promises of the Old Testament.
From Abraham to David, God kept his promise through people who did not deserve it, including a wronged Canaanite widow, a Canaanite of Jericho, and a Moabite.
From David to the exile the royal line decays through good and wicked kings until the throne is lost; God's promise outlives the failure of those who carried it.
After the exile the line goes quiet through forgotten names, yet the count of fourteens shows God keeping time until the Christ, the true son of David.
Joseph faces public shame and a legal duty, and chooses a righteousness that keeps the law without cruelty.
God's word through the angel turns Joseph's plan: the child is from the Holy Spirit, and his name, Jesus, means he will save his people from their sins.
Isaiah's sign to David's house comes to its fullness: the virgin's son is Immanuel, God with us.
Joseph's quiet obedience, taking Mary home and naming the child, makes Jesus legally a son of David.

teach.pitfalls:
The first mistake is to skip the genealogy as filler. It is Matthew's opening argument, and it should be taught as a story told in names. The second is to preach the four women as four sinful women. Tamar is called more righteous than Judah, Rahab is honored for her faith (Hebrews 11:31), Ruth is a model of loyal love, and Bathsheba is named as Uriah's wife precisely to point to David's sin (2 Samuel 12:7-9); calling her an adulteress blames the one with the least power.

The third mistake is to treat Isaiah 7:14 as an isolated proof text with no meaning for Ahaz. Teaching it that way leaves listeners defenseless when a skeptic points out the context. Show the sign in Isaiah 7 and 8, the promised king of Isaiah 9, and how Matthew reads the whole passage. The fourth is to turn verse 25 into a polemic about Mary's perpetual virginity; the verse's point is that Jesus was not Joseph's son by nature, and Christians who differ on Mary's later life can agree on that. Finally, do not sentimentalize Immanuel into a vague sense that God is near. The name belongs to a specific person, and the chapter ties it to a mission: saving his people from their sins.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on family shame. Many people carry histories of abuse, adultery, illegitimacy, or a parent who left, and the genealogy speaks gently to them: God worked through such stories and did not edit them out. Teach Bathsheba's and Tamar's stories carefully, since some listeners were wronged as they were. The story of Joseph and Mary also touches people who have faced an unplanned pregnancy, a broken engagement, or suspicion from those closest to them. Joseph's adoption of Jesus gives dignity to adoptive parents and stepparents, and to people raised without a father: the Son of God was raised by a man who was not his father by blood.

hard.q: Did Isaiah 7:14 predict a virgin birth, and is the virgin conception history or legend?
hard.a:
The objection has a textual form and a historical one. The textual form is ancient and Jewish. Trypho in Justin's Dialogue (67, 71) argued that Isaiah's Hebrew word, almah, means a young woman of marriageable age and not specifically a virgin (Hebrew has a more precise word, bethulah), that the three Jewish Greek translations of the second century (Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion) rendered it ‘young woman’, and that the sign concerned a child born in Ahaz's own day, since Isaiah says that before the boy knows good from evil the two kings Ahaz feared would be gone (Isaiah 7:16). Medieval Jewish commentators such as Rashi and David Kimhi took the mother to be the prophet's wife or the king's. The historical form is modern. Gerd Lüdemann (Virgin Birth?, 1998) argued that the story arose to cover an illegitimate birth; Jane Schaberg (1987) that Matthew knew such a tradition; and others that the story follows ancient legends of great men born of gods, like the tale Suetonius tells of Augustus (Augustus 94). Andrew Lincoln (Born of a Virgin?, 2013), writing as a Christian scholar, argued that the infancy narratives are not meant to be read as a literal biological account.

Responses begin with Isaiah. Almah is never clearly used in the Hebrew Bible of a married woman; it describes Rebekah before marriage (Genesis 24:43) and Moses' sister (Exodus 2:8), and the Jewish translators of the Septuagint chose parthenos two or three centuries before Christ. Interpreters then divide. Some hold that the sign had a first fulfillment in Isaiah's day (perhaps in the child of Isaiah 8:3) and a fuller one in Jesus, in keeping with how Matthew reads Hosea 11:1 in the next chapter. Others, such as Alec Motyer (The Prophecy of Isaiah, 1993), argue that the child who is Immanuel is the royal child of Isaiah 9:6-7, never born in Ahaz's day. Either way, Matthew does not derive the virgin conception from Isaiah; he reads Isaiah in light of an event. On the history, J. Gresham Machen (The Virgin Birth of Christ, 1930) and Raymond Brown (The Birth of the Messiah, 1977) noted that Matthew and Luke tell independent stories that agree on this point, that pagan tales of divine fathers describe a god's sexual union with a woman rather than a conception without intercourse, and that first-century Judaism had no expectation of a virgin-born Messiah that would have invited invention. Brown concluded that historical method alone cannot settle the question. The church confesses in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary; how Isaiah's sign related to Ahaz's day remains a question on which faithful interpreters differ.

hard.q: Why does Matthew's genealogy differ from Luke's, and doesn't the curse on Jeconiah disqualify Jesus from David's throne?
hard.a:
The objection is pressed by critics and by Jewish writers alike. Bart Ehrman (Jesus, Interrupted, 2009) is one of many who note that Matthew and Luke give different fathers for Joseph (Jacob and Heli), follow different sons of David (Solomon and Nathan), and give different numbers of generations, and that Matthew's count of fourteens requires leaving out known kings. Jewish counter-missionary writers add two further objections: tribal descent passes through the father, so if Joseph was not Jesus' father Jesus is not a son of David, and Jeremiah 22:30 says of Jeconiah that none of his descendants will prosper to sit on David's throne, so a Messiah in his line would be disqualified.

Responses take several forms. On the two lists, Julius Africanus (early third century) proposed a levirate marriage that gave Joseph a legal and a natural father; many since the Reformation have held that Luke traces Mary's line, noting that Luke introduces the list with the words “He was regarded as the son of Joseph” (Luke 3:23); others that Matthew gives the royal succession and Luke the natural descent. Critical scholars such as Raymond Brown doubt any harmonization and read each list as a theological statement using the traditions available. On Matthew's omissions, ancient genealogies often skipped generations, and Matthew tells the reader openly that he has arranged the list. On adoption, Joseph's naming of the child made him legally Joseph's son and heir, which is exactly the point of verses 20 to 25. On Jeconiah, Jeremiah's words limit the curse to prosperity in his lifetime and to his immediate line; Haggai 2:23 later calls his grandson Zerubbabel God's chosen signet ring, reversing the image of Jeremiah 22:24; and a rabbinic tradition in the Pesikta de-Rav Kahana holds that God accepted Jeconiah's repentance and set the decree aside. Some add that if Jesus was not Joseph's son by blood, the curse on Jeconiah's offspring does not touch him, while the legal right to the throne does. None of these answers commands universal agreement, and Christians who hold a high view of Scripture differ on which is best.

observe: Which four women does the genealogy name, and how is the fourth named? What do you know of each from the Old Testament?
Where does the repeated pattern ‘A was the father of B’ change in verse 16, and what does the change say about Joseph?
What two names is the child given in verses 21 to 25, who gives each, and what does each mean?
interpret: Why might Matthew make the exile to Babylon one of the three turning points of Israel's history, and what does that suggest the Messiah has come to do?
Verse 19 says Joseph was righteous and unwilling to disgrace Mary. What kind of righteousness is Matthew describing?
How does reading Isaiah 7 to 9 in full change your understanding of the Immanuel sign that Matthew quotes?
apply: The genealogy includes scandal, failure, and forgotten names. What would it mean for you to believe that God can work through your family's history as it actually is?
Joseph obeyed a word that cost him his reputation. Where might obedience to God cost you the good opinion of others?
If Jesus is God with us, what difference does that make to the place where you feel most alone this week?
